title: “Slendro”: Indonesian Gamelan in Prelude, Fugue, and Postlude No.1, Book II
content_blocks: A gamelan is an ensemble of musicians and instruments—like an orchestra. The instruments of the gamelan include at least two types of metallophones—one type with bars or small circular bells spread out over a wooden, resonating frame, another a set of large suspended gongs—and hand drums. It may also include bamboo flutes and other types of percussion instruments, as well as vocalists. Gamelan music is often used for ceremonial, ritual, or theatrical performances, and is often used to accompany dancers.

Different gamelan ensembles will be tuned to different scales.  These scales often feature considerable variability in tuning, and typically are used for different purposes.  The tuning system for this prelude and fugue pair is meant to emulate the five-tone (pentatonic) Slendro scale of Javanese Gamelan.  The tones of this scale are spread quite evenly across the octave, with all of the intervals close to two-and-one-half semitones in size.  Slendro tuning is typically used to accompany older-style shadow puppet plays.

The prelude of this gamelan-inspired piece may be thought of as a solo “exhortation” or call to action.  It establishes the mode, and announces that the ensemble movement is about to begin.  The fugue is the full gamelan ensemble, including bamboo flute and women’s voices (at the beginning and ending of the piece), metallophones of different sizes and ranges, and low gongs punctuating the melodic phrases.  Although there is joy in the music, it is meant to be solemn.

Much gamelan music features “colotomic structure,” in which there are faster time cycles nested within slower time cycles, the faster time cycles typically being in higher instruments, slower time cycles in lower instruments, and the slowest time cycle in the low-pitched gongs (which mark off the end of each cycle).  Since the music played at each of these cyclic levels is often similar, this may be thought of as inherently fugal, in which the different fugal voices start at the same time but at different rates (just as we saw with the prelude of the “Mechanical Motion” set, which I wrote about earlier).  That is precisely what happens in this fugue:  the melody, first introduced by the flute and women’s voices (here portrayed by whistling and piano), is then stated simultaneously at three different rates—the highest is the fastest—and punctuated by the low-pitched gong-like harmonics.

Steve Beck handles the rapid notes of the Prelude and the intricate counterpoint of the Fugue beautifully and easily, as you can see in this combined video of the Prelude and Fugue. Steve is whistling while playing in the video at the start and end of the Fugue, although for the recording I provided an overdubbed whistling part. Steve also demonstrates some keyboard pyrotechnics, such as about 1’10” in to the Prelude, and at several spots in the Fugue as well.

Fun fact about the recording and the preparations: for reasons that aren’t clear to me, some of the poster putty that I used to detune the strings (to approximate a Slendro tuning) also resulted in some tinkly overtones, sounding like a triangle or a crotale. Detuning the strings on my smaller piano at home was far easier than on the larger Steinway used in the recording, but I didn’t get any of those bell-like overtones at home, so this was a pleasant surprise. Listen for them at various spots during the fugue, especially in the second half.
Steve whistles while playing at the start and end of the Fugue.
